topStories.headline: Potrero Hill Apartment Complex Sells for $132M in City's Priciest Multifamily Deal in Two Years
topStories.dek: Stockbridge Capital Group's acquisition of Alta Potrero reflects surging demand from AI-industry workers priced close to Mission Bay.
topStories.body:
Stockbridge Capital Group has paid $132 million for the 172-unit Alta Potrero apartment complex at 1301 16th Street on Potrero Hill — the most expensive multifamily acquisition in San Francisco on a per-unit basis since 2024. The San Francisco-based investment firm paid just over $767,000 per unit for the studios-to-three-bedroom property, which includes 29 subsidized units and 6,700 square feet of ground-floor retail.

The deal was reported by The Real Deal and confirmed by Hoodline on August 13, 2026. The buyer is listed in public records as SCG 1301 16th Street LLC, a Delaware corporation tied to Stockbridge, with Mark Carlson, Stockbridge's managing director of transactions, named in the filing. Sausalito-based Wood Partners, which broke ground on the project in 2018 and completed it in 2020, was the seller.

Analysts say the sale is the clearest signal yet that institutional buyers will pay a steep premium for newly built rental housing steps from San Francisco's booming AI employers. OpenAI and Y Combinator have contributed to rising housing demand in Potrero Hill, with the neighborhood attracting high-paid employees seeking quieter housing close to Mission Bay offices. Compass data shows Potrero Hill homes have been selling at 42 percent over asking amid what some real estate observers have dubbed the 'Area AI' effect.

The transaction arrives amid a broader city debate over San Francisco's 6 percent transfer tax on real estate sales of $25 million or more. Mayor Daniel Lurie and Supervisor Bilal Mahmood introduced the BUILD Act earlier in 2026 to cut that tax in half, arguing it would encourage more institutional investment and accelerate housing production.

topStories.headline: SoMa's Foundry Ditches Corporate Events for EDM and Phone-Free Dance Floors
topStories.dek: New ownership is transforming the Folsom Street venue into a music-forward nightclub set to reopen August 22.
topStories.body:
A team of Bay Area nightlife veterans is taking over the Foundry at 1425 Folsom Street in SoMa and pivoting the 4,400-square-foot venue away from corporate retreats toward electronic dance music and community programming. Andrew Wasilewski, who co-founded the Faight Collective artist space in Lower Haight, signed the final paperwork July 31 with a group of music industry professionals and is now the incoming owner and general manager, according to the San Francisco Standard.

The Folsom Street Foundry stopped operations July 27 and is expected to reopen August 22. Wasilewski told the Chronicle that the new operators plan a mix of electronic music — from listening parties to full DJ nights — along with lectures, dating events, and falafel and kabobs. A cornerstone of the relaunch is a phone-free dance floor policy, with community guidelines emphasizing presence, consent, and respect.

The first announced lineup under new leadership includes Italian DJ Kybba on September 18, New York sibling duo Tinzo and Jojo for a two-night run October 24–25, and Florida-based producer Wonkywilla on October 30. On weeknights, the team plans to program listening parties and ambient music events where attendees bring their own records to play on the venue's sound system.

The pivot arrives as SoMa's nightlife scene navigates significant volatility; nearby drag club Oasis announced its closure at 11th and Folsom in July 2025. The Foundry building itself dates to 1936, constructed as an Art Deco brick warehouse in what is now Western SoMa's Light Industrial Historic District.

topStories.headline: SF Planning Department Poised to Rule on Prologis's $8B Fourth & King Railyard Megaproject
topStories.dek: The ambitious 20-acre mixed-use development at the Caltrain terminus would stitch together SoMa, Mission Bay, and Showplace Square with 2,500 homes and a towering transit hub.
topStories.body:
The San Francisco Planning Department is moving toward a decision on developer Prologis's application to remake the Caltrain railyard at Fourth and King Street into a dense, mixed-use district featuring roughly 2,500 residences, approximately four million square feet of commercial space, and an 850-foot mixed-use tower rising directly above a rebuilt Caltrain station. The Potrero View reported in June 2026 that a planning approval is imminent, following the city's April publication of a complete application notice that established a formal decision deadline.

Prologis, best known for warehouse logistics real estate, submitted the application to the Planning Department in March 2026 in a joint venture with Caltrain. At full build-out — projected at 15 to 20 years — the project would encompass between 7 and 8 million square feet including the commercial and residential components. The redeveloped site would also include a promenade on Townsend Street, a public plaza on 5th Street, and a park on 6th Street.

Supporters argue the project would physically reconnect the SoMa, Showplace Square, and Mission Bay neighborhoods, which the current railyard effectively divides. The site is also expected to serve as the city's gateway to the California High-Speed Rail network. Mayor Daniel Lurie said in a statement that the project 'will continue that momentum up into SoMa, leading with public space and transit access.'

Caltrain spokesperson Dan Lieberman said the project does not propose changes to current Caltrain service, though temporary schedule adjustments could be necessary during construction. Environmental review of the proposal is underway.

moreNews.headline: Potrero Hill's 'Area AI' Housing Boom Spreads to Dogpatch
moreNews.body: OpenAI's nearly one-million-square-foot campus in Mission Bay has turned San Francisco's southeastern neighborhoods into what real estate insiders call 'Area AI,' where Potrero Hill homes have been selling 42 percent over asking and condo prices are surging. Compass agent Jerry Rice Jr. told The Real Deal in July that the Dogpatch neighborhood — long characterized by warehouses — is the next beneficiary, with residential prices already creeping upward. The median condo price in the corridor rose 7.3 percent over the past year to $1.1 million, with total condo sales up 15.2 percent.

moreNews.headline: Yerba Buena Gardens Festival Still Going Strong at Midseason
moreNews.body: KALW reported this week that the Yerba Buena Gardens Festival — the only curated arts park in San Francisco fully dedicated to free cultural programming — is barely past its midpoint, with performances continuing through November. Located in the SoMa neighborhood between Mission and Howard Streets, the 26th-season festival offers poetry and dance workshops alongside an eclectic lineup of local and international musical acts several days a week, all free to attend.

moreNews.headline: Dogpatch Arts Hub Minnesota Street Project Welcomes Ruth Asawa Gallery
moreNews.body: The Minnesota Street Project in Dogpatch opened a permanent gallery run by Ruth Asawa Lanier, Inc. this spring, giving San Franciscans a steady place to see the beloved artist's wire sculptures, drawings, and community projects. The 1,714-square-foot space — the first permanent venue providing regular public access to Asawa's looped-wire work — is now open at 1275 Minnesota Street. Multiple exhibitions run through October 3, 2026, with admission free to the public.
